title: Idols from the House
hook: the idols are removed from the Ka'ba as he recites, truth has come and falsehood vanished (17:81)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the people who had driven him out waited for his answer, and he gave them Yusuf's words: no blame on you today. Go, you are free. Did an old grudge loosen at all? Day two hundred seventy-nine.

Think of the Ka'ba the way Muslims describe it: a plain stone house in a valley, which the Qur'an says Abraham and his son Ishmael raised for the worship of the one God. Now picture it on the morning of the conquest. Around it stand idols, the reports say three hundred and sixty of them, belonging to tribes from all over Arabia. Carved stone, wood, painted faces. For generations, pilgrims had come to this house and prayed to all of them. The Prophet ﷺ walks up to them with a stick in his hand. Nobody fights him. Nobody stops him. He's reciting something under his breath. Today, the house gets cleared.
screen: `A HOUSE ABRAHAM RAISED.` → `THREE HUNDRED AND SIXTY IDOLS.` → `A STICK, AND A VERSE.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari records the scene. As he went round the idols, he pointed at them with the stick, or struck them, and they fell, and he recited a verse from the seventeenth surah. In Pickthall's old translation it reads: "Truth hath come and falsehood hath vanished away. Lo! falsehood is ever bound to vanish." Look at the way that verse is built. It doesn't say truth fought falsehood and won after a long war. It says truth came, and falsehood simply went. Like turning on a light: you don't have to drag the dark out of the room. Muslims read the clearing of the Ka'ba as a return, not a new building. In their telling, the house was always meant for one God, and the idols were the add-ons, piled up over centuries. So removing them was a kind of restoration, the house given back to what it was for. The reports add a detail: images inside the Ka'ba were removed too, and he would not enter until they were. And notice what did not happen. The people who had prayed to those idols were the same people he had just set free the day before. The statues came down. The people were let go. Muslim teachers often hold those two side by side: firm about the false thing, gentle with the person who held it. That's a hard balance in any family argument. And the verse keeps a promise inside it: falsehood is bound to vanish. It may take a while. But it doesn't last.
screen: `HE RECITES AS THEY FALL.` · `TRUTH CAME. FALSEHOOD WENT.` · `THE HOUSE GIVEN BACK.` · `FIRM WITH THE IDOL, GENTLE WITH THE PERSON.` · then, large: `TRUTH HATH COME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clear one false thing from your room. Sit first, and look around. Is there something in your space that tells you a lie? A mirror you only use to criticize yourself. A screen that promises rest and never gives it. A note you keep that says you're not enough. Just notice it, and decide what you'll do with it after the bell. If you pray, you can recite the verse under your breath, as he did: truth has come. If you don't, just sit with the room a little clearer. The bell holds the time.
Idols from the House. The day the Ka'ba was cleared, and a verse was recited over every fallen statue. Today's word.
Your line: truth has come. Today, when you catch a small lie, one you tell or one you tell yourself, don't argue with it. Just say the line and let it go. Day two hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims recite 17:81 when speaking of the conquest of Mecca and the clearing of the Ka'ba, and teachers use the scene to explain tawhid: the house restored to the worship of one God.

fork.setup: you're standing before the Ka'ba with three hundred and sixty idols around it and a stick in your hand. what do you say?
options: a speech against the tribes who made them.
a verse: truth hath come and falsehood hath vanished away.
fork.reveal: al-Bukhari records that he recited 17:81 as each one fell. no speech against anyone, just the verse.

original.note: Arabic: truth has come. al-haqq is also one of the names of God: the Real, the True.

trapdoor: what you thought: statues being smashed.
what it means: the house given back to one God, firm with the idol, gentle with the person.
what a scholar hears: al-Bukhari's report puts 17:81 in his mouth at the Ka'ba, a Meccan verse recited years after it came down, now fulfilled in the place it named.

sources.quoted: Truth hath come and falsehood hath vanished away. Lo! falsehood is ever bound to vanish.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4287 (360 idols around the Ka'ba; he struck them reciting 17:81)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4288 (the images inside the Ka'ba removed before he entered)
Qur'an 2:127 (Abraham and Ishmael raise the foundations of the House)

notes: Pickthall wording of 17:81 quoted from memory; check word for word against the 1930 text.
Bukhari 4287/4288 numbering cited from memory; confirm. Reports differ on whether he pointed at or struck the idols; the script says 'pointed at them with the stick, or struck them'.
The trapdoor calls 17:81 a Meccan verse recited years later; surah al-Isra is generally classed as Meccan. Confirm.
The practice's examples (a critical mirror, a screen) are modern pictures of a 'false thing', not a claim about idolatry; confirm the Keeper is comfortable with the analogy.
